newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Gaps remain between heaven and earth in Vietnam.
newsitem.headline: Gaps remain between heaven and earth in Vietnam.

text.p: A high-level Vatican delegation ended a visit to Vietnam on Friday with slim progress to report in a difficult relationship between the Holy See and Hanoi.

In a late-night interview on Thursday papal envoy archbishop Claudio Celli used diplomatic language to describe the results of his five-day trip and said it had succeeded in reviving dialogue stalled for the past 18 months.
"I think the dialogue was open and frank and in a cordial atmosphere," he said. "You could say we're engaged to find a positive solution to problems still pending."
Vietnam has eased controls on religious freedoms in recent years but its communist government and the Vatican have remained at odds over a range of issues, some of which are seen as fundamental.
In a move aimed at propelling relations forward the Holy See reluctantly agreed in 1994 to give Hanoi the right to review church appointments.
Hanoi has not been shy about exercising its power and several bishops' nominations have been turned down.
Celli said no progress had been made on the key and sensitive question of a successor to archbishop Paul Nguyen Van Binh, who died in July last year leaving his Ho Chi Minh City diocese seat vacant.
But he said agreement had been reached on the Vatican's choice of two coadjutor bishops -- effectively a successor to an existing bishop. He did not name the bishops concerned.
Vietnam's 75 million population is majority Buddhist, but its estimated seven million Roman Catholic community is the biggest in East Asia after the Philippines.
Most live in the south, around Ho Chi Minh City, where Catholicism was associated during the Vietnam War with the elite in U.S.-backed Saigon.
Officials at Hanoi's religious affairs department could not be contacted by phone on Friday for comment.
